articles.title: HISTORIC WEEK FOR CANADIAN ENERGY: Pipelines, LNG and Billions in New Investment Move Forward - todayville.com

It has been an unusually consequential week for Canadian energy.
In the space of just a few days, Canada saw a final investment decision to double the country’s largest LNG export facility, progress on moving more crude through the Trans Mountain system, a $1.2-billion federal commitment to marine protection, and, most significantly, Ottawa officially designate the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline as a project of national interest.
Get the Latest Canadian Focused Energy News Delivered to You! It’s FREE: Quick Sign-Up Here
Individually, each announcement matters. Taken together, they suggest something broader: Canada is putting considerably more emphasis on building the infrastructure required to move its energy to international markets.
Pacific Link Gets National-Interest Designation
The biggest announcement came Thursday, October 1, in Fort McMurray.
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced that the proposed West Coast Oil Pipeline, now officially called Pacific Link, has been listed as a project of national interest under the Building Canada Act.
The proposed pipeline would transport approximately one million barrels of crude oil per day from Alberta to British Columbia’s coast, providing substantially greater access to Asia-Pacific markets.
Ottawa says Canada and Alberta would share equal ownership, while Indigenous communities would be offered at least a 10 per cent ownership opportunity supported by federal and provincial Indigenous loan-guarantee programs. The federal government estimates the project could create 140,000 jobs, contribute more than $20 billion annually to GDP and generate $100 billion in government revenues by 2060. Those figures are government projections and will depend on the project’s eventual design, cost and operation.
The designation is not final construction approval. Regulatory work, engineering, Indigenous consultation, permitting, financing and commercial commitments still have to be completed.
But it puts Pacific Link into Ottawa’s accelerated major-project process and represents an important shift from debating whether another West Coast oil pipeline should be considered to determining how one could actually be built.
LNG Canada Phase 2 Gets the Green Light
Just days earlier came another enormous decision.
The partners in LNG Canada — Shell, PETRONAS, PetroChina, Mitsubishi and KOGAS — made their final investment decision on Phase 2 of the Kitimat, B.C., LNG project.
Phase 2 will double LNG Canada’s capacity from approximately 14 million tonnes annually to 28 million tonnes, potentially positioning the facility among the world’s larger LNG export operations. Construction is expected to create as many as 4,000 jobs at its peak.
Unlike a proposed project awaiting investors, this is a final investment decision backed by some of the world’s largest energy companies.
That distinction is important.
Canada spent years discussing its potential to export LNG to Asia while the United States and other countries built facilities and captured market share. LNG Canada’s first phase began exports in 2025. Phase 2 means Canada is now substantially expanding that presence.
Trans Mountain Gets More Commercial Certainty
There was important news for Canada’s existing West Coast oil export system as well.
On September 29, the Canada Energy Regulator approved a negotiated settlement covering tolls, tariffs and transportation service on the Trans Mountain Pipeline System.
Under the agreement, firm contracted capacity will increase from 80 per cent to 90 per cent of the system’s nominal capacity, with implementation targeted for January 1, 2027.
That provides Trans Mountain and its shippers with greater long-term commercial certainty following completion of the pipeline expansion.
Meanwhile, dredging has begun in the Second Narrows area of Burrard Inlet. The work is intended to improve navigation and potentially allow vessels serving facilities east of the Ironworkers Memorial Bridge,  including Trans Mountain’s Westridge Marine Terminal, to sail with fuller loads.
It sounds like a comparatively small infrastructure project beside a new pipeline or LNG terminal, but moving more crude on each tanker can improve the efficiency of Canada’s existing export infrastructure.
Ottawa Links More Trade With More Marine Protection
Greater energy exports inevitably mean greater marine traffic.
Ottawa responded this week by announcing $1.2 billion in additional ocean-protection measures, including marine monitoring, science, spill preparedness, Coast Guard capabilities, search and rescue infrastructure and protection of marine ecosystems.
Carney explicitly connected the investment with Canada’s plans to expand West Coast trade and energy infrastructure.
The government is describing its approach as effectively protecting marine environments while expanding Canada’s ability to trade.
That will be particularly important if Pacific Link proceeds and tanker traffic from the Vancouver area increases substantially.
Something Bigger May Be Happening
Any one of these announcements could have commanded a week’s worth of attention.
Instead, Canada received all of them almost simultaneously.
LNG Canada Phase 2 represents billions of dollars of additional private investment. Trans Mountain is gaining greater commercial certainty and potentially improved marine efficiency. Ottawa is investing in the infrastructure needed to manage increasing vessel traffic. And Pacific Link has crossed an important federal threshold toward potentially giving Western Canadian oil another major route to world markets.
There remain major challenges. Pacific Link still has to navigate regulatory reviews, Indigenous consultation, financing, construction risk and producer commitments. Large energy projects remain expensive, complicated and politically contentious.
But this week produced something the Canadian energy industry has often argued has been missing: forward movement on several fronts at once.
For Canada, that could be significant.
A country with enormous oil and natural-gas resources benefits when it has multiple customers, multiple export routes and infrastructure capable of connecting Canadian production with global demand. LNG exports to Asia, additional oil capacity to the Pacific and a more efficiently utilized Trans Mountain system all point toward greater diversification beyond Canada’s traditional dependence on the United States.
The test now will be execution.
But after years when Canadian energy discussions were frequently dominated by projects being delayed, cancelled or debated indefinitely, this week offered a distinctly different storyline: Canada is increasingly talking about how to build and several very large energy projects are actually moving forward.

Oil Prices Fall as Europe Weighs Emergency Reserve Release Under U.S. Pressure
Oil prices dropped sharply on Friday as Europe edged closer to another emergency release of strategic reserves, a move encouraged by the Trump administration. According to Oilprice, West Texas Intermediate fell nearly 4% while Brent slipped below the $100 mark.
At 6:54 a.m. ET, WTI was trading at $89.36, down 3.78%, and Brent stood at $99.79 per barrel, down 2.46%.
The decline came after reports that European governments are weighing a coordinated drawdown of emergency oil stocks, with Washington pressing allies to supply more crude and diesel to ease a global fuel crunch.
European Energy Commissioner Dan Jorgensen said discussions were under way with all members of the International Energy Agency, not only the United States, about the right moment to release reserves. He noted that such releases had been used before and would likely be used again, describing a strategic reserve release as one possibility for curbing high fuel prices.
An EU source told Euronews that the European Commission held a call on Thursday with several countries, including the non-EU country the UK, to assess different scenarios amid intensifying U.S. pressure.
Sources close to the discussions told Reuters on Thursday that the U.S. administration has urged Germany and France, Europe's largest economies and holders of a sizeable share of the EU's emergency reserves, to release diesel from emergency stockpiles or face a potential U.S. diesel export ban.
Crude oil prices had jumped again in September to above $100 per barrel, and global fuel markets, especially for diesel, continued to tighten, with diesel prices hitting record highs in many countries, including the United States.
Germany and France together hold about 35% of the EU's strategic diesel reserves. The EU is estimated to hold about 39 million tons of diesel, equivalent to more than two months of consumption for the bloc.
The United States is pressing European countries that have not released all the emergency stocks pledged under the IEA-led drawdown in the early weeks of the Iran war to do so now.
Earlier this week, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said that while the United States and Japan are delivering on their commitments, several European member countries have released only a fraction of the crude oil and petroleum products they pledged, and he urged every member country to fulfill its commitments.

articles.title: Hidden Uranium in DRC Cobalt Exports to China: Is It a Problem? - The China-Global South Project
articles.summary: Hidden Uranium in DRC Cobalt Exports to China: Is It a Problem?  The China-Global South Project
articles.full_text:
The DRC’s cobalt industry is also moving uranium through global supply chains, creating a problem that extends beyond critical-minerals security. Researchers estimate that 2,000–5,000 tons of uranium may have left the country as a byproduct of cobalt production, raising questions about nuclear-security risks, environmental exposure, and the traceability of mineral exports.
The challenge is persistent rather than catastrophic: uranium occurs naturally alongside DRC cobalt and can remain in cobalt hydroxide even when companies follow existing processing standards. Weak shipment-level monitoring and inconsistent reporting leave uncertainty over where the uranium goes and how it is handled after reaching China and other markets.
Ryan Manzuk, Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Program on Science and Global Security, joins Cobus and Geraud to analyze uranium contamination in DRC cobalt exports, including nuclear-security implications, environmental and worker exposure, and measures to improve traceability and local processing.
Show Notes
- Nature Communications: Uranium in cobalt-hydroxide exports from the Democratic Republic of the Congo by Ryan A. Manzuk & Sébastien Philippe
📌 Topics Covered in This Episode
- Uranium contamination in DRC cobalt exports
- China’s role in cobalt supply chains
- Nuclear security risks from uranium exports
- Environmental and health risks for miners
- Traceability, regulation, and local processing
About Ryan Manzuk
Ryan A. Manzuk is a Postdoctoral Research Associate in the Program on Science and Global Security at Princeton University and is affiliated with the Department of Nuclear Engineering and Engineering Physics at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. His research applies scientific and computational methods to investigate critical events and develop data-driven perspectives on contemporary security, conflict, and environmental challenges.
Manzuk received his PhD in Geosciences from Princeton University in 2024, where his doctoral research focused primarily on sedimentary geology. His graduate work also incorporated novel remote sensing techniques to examine conflict-related issues, in partnership with SITU Studio in Brooklyn, New York. He holds a bachelor’s degree from the University of Chicago and previously spent two years as a Peace Corps Volunteer in Guinea, where he worked on sustainable and climate-adaptive agricultural solutions.
At Princeton, Manzuk’s current research examines whether safeguards against the mining of uranium are being upheld. His work also considers communities located near uranium-rich ores, with a focus on understanding and constraining potential health and environmental consequences. His broader research interests include remote sensing, computational image analysis, human rights violations, conflict zones, and the application of Earth-science methods to contemporary global security challenges.

articles.title: Mapping Critical Minerals in the UAE: Strategic Demand, Supply Gaps and Climate Trade-Offs - orfme.org
articles.summary: Mapping Critical Minerals in the UAE: Strategic Demand, Supply Gaps and Climate Trade-Offs  orfme.org
articles.full_text:
Spotlight
- The UAE needs a national critical minerals list and cannot borrow one from the IEA, USGS or EU.
- The UAE’s mineral demand has two tiers—broad/recurrent minerals like copper, aluminium, and steel for existing infrastructure and narrow/irreplaceable minerals such as lithium, cobalt, and REEs tied to the transition targets.
- The UAE is working towards closing the supply gap. Currently, it is stronger for aluminium, copper, and lithium but absent for titanium, PGMs, gallium, and tantalum.
Critical minerals have gained considerable prominence in government economic and national security agendas. This increased focus has emerged from concerns over supply-chain concentration and geopolitical exposure, be it the Chinese export restrictions on rare earth elements (REEs) or conflict-driven disruptions in the Middle East. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is responding by leveraging its financial capital and geographic position to secure supply chains, even though it has limited mineral wealth of its own and remains structurally import dependent for raw-material processing.
Despite their significance to its industrial growth ambitions, the UAE still lacks a national critical minerals list. Adopting a critical minerals list from the United States Geological Survey (USGS), European Union (EU), or International Energy Agency (IEA) would not work for the UAE as a hydrocarbon-rich, mineral-poor economy pursuing rapid diversification. This article identifies which minerals are critical for the nation by mapping mineral demand across its strategic sectors and examines its supply position vis-à-vis these.
A UAE-Specific Approach to Criticality
The relevance of critical minerals to the UAE’s economic growth stems from its strategic commitments. These include Operation 300 bn, the Energy Strategy 2050, the National Space Strategy 2030, the Dubai Industrial Strategy 2030, and the Etihad Rail, among others, in policy areas on circular economy, green growth, industry, and artificial intelligence (AI).
These policies identify 24 sectors (see Table 1) across energy, resource security, advanced manufacturing, trade and logistics, infrastructure, and advanced technology that the UAE is focusing on and that have large material requirements. The 24 sectors were mapped against the individual minerals that each depends on to build a mineral-by-sector matrix of critical minerals for the UAE. This list measures criticality by how often the mineral occurs across UAE’s strategic sectors. Due to the non-availability of data, criticality is not measured by the volume of the mineral required or its supply chain.
- The energy mix includes the electricity grid, battery storage and Electric Vehicles (EVs), traditional hydrocarbons, solar, nuclear, and hydrogen. These form the baseline of the UAE’s transition and diversification agenda using the widest spread of minerals.
- The agri-tech and water desalination sectors provide resource security. They have a smaller mineral footprint but are crucial for the country. Advanced manufacturing sectors include defence, aerospace, maritime, pharmaceuticals, food processing, and machinery and equipment. These have been split into two distinct types of demands—sectors with existing capacity including aluminium and fabricated metals, food processing, and pharmaceuticals; and sectors where the mineral demand is tied to the UAE’s future targets including defence, aerospace, and maritime.
- The trade and logistics, as well as infrastructure sectors, including shipping, ports, aviation, roads, railways, and construction, are mineral-light and already served by existing steel and aluminium supply chains.
- The advanced technology and AI sectors (semiconductors, space, and data centres) are the newest and fastest growing but also the most speculative categories. Data-centre demand is real and current while semiconductor demand remains contingent on the UAE’s chip-manufacturing ambitions.
Table 1: The UAE’s Strategic Sections: A Mineral-Wise Breakdown
Source: UAE’s Strategic Sectors.
Note: Mineral input requirements for each sector were identified from technical and industry literature on end-use applications of critical minerals, including IEA sectoral reports, USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries, and sector-specific engineering and industry sources.
Table 1 measures criticality by recurrence, which is only one dimension. It does not encapsulate how essential a mineral is within the sectors or how concentrated is its global supply. Judging purely by recurrence, copper, iron and steel, and aluminium dominate the matrix, but going by strategic intensity and supply risk, minerals that appear in only one or two sectors, such as lithium, are equally critical. Hence, the matrix helps identify two tiers rather than a single ranking.
- Tier 1—Broad/ Recurrent Minerals: Copper (20), iron and steel (19), aluminium (18), REEs (10), nickel (9), and titanium (8) recur across most of the UAE’s strategic sectors, including grid, infrastructure, defence, aerospace, and space, making them critical. Since the UAE imports raw minerals entirely and does not have any domestic mineral wealth, criticality is a function of their occurrence across sectors. A supply gap in any of these minerals would stall multiple sectors simultaneously.
- Tier 2—Concentrated, Low-Substitutability Minerals: Lithium, cobalt, Platinum Group Metals (PGMs), gallium and tantalum recur in fewer sectors but each of these is the most crucial input for its respective sector. Lithium and cobalt are crucial to battery storage and EV targets under the Energy Strategy 2050 and the Net Zero 2050 strategy. PGMs are necessary for green hydrogen, while gallium and tantalum are necessary for defence electronics and semiconductors. The global supply for each mineral is concentrated in a small number of producing and processing countries with few or no substitutes available with existing technology. Their criticality is a function of their depth, and a shortfall would stall the specific industry targets.
Both tiers point to two different kinds of exposures for the UAE. Tier 1 covers the existing infrastructure and industrial base while Tier 2 covers the UAE’s forward-looking transition and diversification agenda. Identifying what the country needs is only half the picture; securing the necessary material is the other.
The UAE’s Supply Position: Mining, Processing, and Overseas Access
Separating the UAE’s position according to upstream access, midstream capacity, and downstream recovery makes it clearer where the country’s supply chains are genuinely secure and where they remain exposed.
Upstream: Raw Material Access
Within the Tier 1 minerals, UAE has the strongest capacity for aluminium. It can acquire aluminium through the Emirates Global Aluminium (EGA) bauxite operations in Guinea and also has domestic alumina refining and smelting capacities, completing the mineral value chain.
For other critical minerals, upstream access has largely been built through overseas equity rather than domestic reserves. In February 2026, Abu Dhabi’s International Resources Holding (IRH) acquired a 51 percent controlling stake in Zambia’s Mopani Copper Mines. The UAE also has a share in copper cathodes produced by the Democratic Republic of Congo’s (DRC) state mining company, Gecamines. Additionally, IRH acquired a majority stake in DRC’s Alphamin Resources mining in one of the world’s largest tin deposits. The UAE has also begun building upstream access for REEs. New Energi Metals Holdings (NEM) signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Indonesia in 2026 to explore niobium and REEs in Gabon and Indonesia.
On the other hand, nickel and titanium have no upstream or midstream domestic capacity in the UAE; there is complete import dependency for both. Additionally, the UAE has no domestic uranium reserves and no enrichment capability under the 2009 bilateral nuclear cooperation agreement and non-proliferation policy with the US. The Barakah Nuclear Energy Plant’s fuel security is met entirely through long-term supply contracts with external producers. The UAE cannot close this processing gap through investments and building infrastructure.
Midstream: Processing and Refining
Iron ore is not domestically mined in the UAE, creating an upstream gap, but its EMSTEEL Group operates a domestic integrated steel plant using imported ore and pellets. Similarly, the UAE-based Titan Lithium has built a processing plant in Abu Dhabi Khalifa Industrial Area, producing battery-grade lithium compounds from ore sources in Zimbabwe. It has also signed a supply agreement with Mercedes-Benz for EVs, building midstream capacity for lithium. The UAE is also building midstream capacity for cobalt with DRC with a copper-cobalt refinery. PGMs, gallium and tantalum currently have no domestic mining, processing, or partnerships.
Downstream: Circular Recovery
Circular recovery is another way to secure mineral value chains. EGA acquired assets in 2024 for aluminium recycling in Europe. EMSTEEL has also signed an MoU on circular steel production through scrap and waste recovery. There was also a joint venture in January 2026 between MoEI-BEEAH-LOHUM for recovering lithium, cobalt, and nickel from end-of-life batteries. The UAE also has a commercial scrap sector across copper, aluminium, and steel.
Beyond specific mineral partnerships, the UAE has also signed an MoU with the US on critical minerals cooperation and similar agreements with India, Canada, Australia, Argentina, and Uzbekistan.
Closing the Gap: Towards a National Critical Minerals List
There is a gap between the demand and supply of these minerals in the UAE. Several of the minerals that the nation depends on are ones for which no domestic, offshore, or circular access has yet been built, compounding their criticality.

OPEC+ Expected to Hold November Quotas Steady at Weekend Meeting
Key OPEC+ producers are expected to keep their crude oil output quotas for November unchanged at a meeting this weekend, according to anonymous sources cited by Reuters on Wednesday. The report, carried by Reuters, indicates that no change to the group's current targets is anticipated.
Gulf producers within OPEC+ have been pumping and shipping considerably smaller volumes since the Iran war disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. At the early September monthly meeting, Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria, and Oman chose to hold the September 2026 required production quotas in place for October 2026, after unwinding a combined 1.65 million barrels per day of collective cuts that started in 2023.
OPEC+ has lifted nominal production quotas through most of this year, yet actual supply reaching the market has stayed well under required output levels because of the Middle East conflict. Crude production in many Gulf states has fallen substantially short of OPEC+ quotas, which have largely ceased to be meaningful since March, as the Strait of Hormuz disruptions locked a significant share of supply inside the Persian Gulf.
The producer group, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia, appears to have turned its attention to debates and discussions over 2027 quotas, with the alliance planning to review and establish baselines for any future cuts.
In recent weeks, OPEC oil production declined in August on lower Saudi supply, while output among the core OPEC+ producers rose. Saudi Arabia's oil production dropped in August amid Houthi threats to shipments in the Red Sea, pulling OPEC output lower, a Bloomberg survey showed.
OPEC data in its September Monthly Oil Market Report showed total crude oil production across the entire OPEC+ alliance averaged 38.05 million barrels per day in August 2026, an increase of 300,000 barrels per day from July. OPEC+ production remains roughly 5 million barrels per day below pre-war levels, as nearly all OPEC Gulf members are trailing their quotas because of continuing shipping disruptions.

Shafaq News- Baghdad
OPEC+ has delayed a review of members’ 2027 oil production capacity after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted expansion projects across the Middle East, Reuters reported on Friday, citing two sources close to the matter.
Originally due by the end of September, the assessment is now expected to be completed by mid-November, according to one source. The findings will establish how much crude each member can sustainably produce and serve as a reference for setting 2027 production baselines.
The war has disrupted expansion projects in several OPEC+ countries, complicating estimates of future output. Some members have also yet to provide the information required for the process, although the Reuters sources did not identify them.
US petroleum consultancy DeGolyer and MacNaughton is evaluating participating countries except Russia, Iran, and Venezuela, which are under US sanctions. Its findings are expected to reach OPEC ahead of the alliance’s next group-wide meeting later in November. Lower sustainable capacity could result in smaller allocations, while producers that have expanded output potential could seek higher baselines.
The process is particularly important for Iraq, OPEC’s second-largest crude producer, which has long argued that its current quota does not account for increased capacity. Government sources told Shafaq News in June that Baghdad was seeking a higher allocation and had considered leaving OPEC, although the Oil Ministry denied any plan to withdraw and reaffirmed Iraq’s commitment to the organization.
Crude sales generate roughly 90% of Iraq’s state revenue, leaving public finances highly exposed to output restrictions and disruptions along export routes. Around 93% to 95% of the country’s oil exports normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz, which has remained almost entirely closed since the regional war began in February 2026.
Baghdad has also repeatedly exceeded its OPEC+ ceiling and submitted compensation plans to offset excess production, an issue it shares with Kazakhstan. The dispute has gained greater significance as Iraq seeks to recover revenue lost during months of export disruption while negotiating future production limits in an unsettled oil market.
Leaving OPEC would free Iraq from the group’s production limits, although withdrawals remain relatively rare. Angola exited in early 2024 following a quota dispute, after Qatar in 2019, Ecuador in 2020, and Indonesia in 2016, while the UAE withdrew in 2026.

articles.summary: [EP.1] Critical minerals: A recourse waiting for a strategy  Telquel.ma
articles.full_text:
Critical and strategic minerals are making headlines in the business press and have become indispensable to many industries, from automotive and energy to information and communication technology (ICT). Copper is a good example, as is silicon, which is needed for photovoltaic panels, while titanium is vital for the aerospace industry and lithium for electric vehicle batteries.
These valuable minerals are a source of concern for major economic powers, which are now seeking to secure their supply chains, a critical imperative at a time when China is exerting a stranglehold on their production and processing.
With its mineral resources, Morocco has a role to play in this international competition. Last February, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated that the Kingdom had a “key role” to play in diversifying supply chains for critical minerals.
Strategic or critical minerals?
First and foremost, it is essential to understand what we are talking about and to distinguish between critical minerals and strategic minerals. During a lecture at the Dhar El Mahraz Faculty of Sciences in Fez in November 2025, geological engineer Addi Azza emphasized that a strategic mineral is essential to a state’s economic interests, defense, or energy policy, or even to the operations of a specific industrial player.
But the criticality of a raw material, whether rock or metal, depends on the difficulty of securing its supply. This difficulty can cause prices to skyrocket and weigh heavily on industry or the wider economy. Sabrine Emran, a senior economist at the Policy Center for the New South (PCNS), explains the factors involved: the geographic concentration of global supply, geopolitical risks, the potential for substitution and recycling, and a country’s dependence on imports. All of these elements help determine the criticality of a mineral.
Minerals considered critical or strategic therefore vary from one country to another: each has its own definition, based on its interests, the importance of the material in its industrial production chain, its level of scarcity, the situation in the supplying country, or the concentration of production in a few countries.
Morocco: Still lacking a framework
But in Morocco, the situation remains unclear. The Kingdom “does not yet have an official, consolidated legal definition of critical and strategic minerals, nor a specific regulatory list” says Sabrine Emran. Yet the mining sector is in the process of reinventing itself. Leïla Benali, Minister of Energy Transition and Sustainable Development, spoke of a “new era” during the presentation, in late 2025, of the ministry’s strategy to reposition the mining sector at the heart of the Moroccan economy.
Law 33.13 on mining must be reformed to modernize the sector. Bill 72.24 was thus submitted in November 2025 to the General Secretariat of the Government. The bill also includes a section dedicated to critical and strategic minerals, with the creation of a national technical committee tasked with “monitoring their supply and ensuring that their extraction contributes to Morocco’s industrial sovereignty, while coordinating the various relevant public policies” says the PCNS economist.
Nevertheless, its exact role and the terms of its implementation must be clarified, given the absence of an official timeline. This uncertainty is all the more pressing as legislative elections approach. “The next government could decide to continue the reform along its current lines, modify it, or opt for a different approach to the governance of strategic and critical minerals” emphasizes Sabrine Emran.
Drawing on international standards
From a technical standpoint, this mining reform can draw on international standards, notes Sabrine Emran. She cites CRIRSCO, a global organization responsible for developing standards for the mining sector, as well as the UNFC, a universal system for the classification and management of mineral and energy resources under the auspices of the United Nations. “CRIRSCO helps improve the comparability and transparency of data related to exploration, resources, and reserves, while the UNFC provides a broader framework for resource classification” she explains.
Above all, these standards ensure the quality and comparability of geological and economic information, even though Morocco’s priorities must remain at the heart of this classification. Sabrine Emran specifically mentions the rapidly evolving needs related to batteries, electrical infrastructure, green hydrogen, aerospace, defense, and, now, artificial intelligence.
An initial list from the CESE
At this stage, only an initiative by the Economic, Social, and Environmental Council (CESE), dating from 2023, has outlined a list of 24 minerals, including aluminum, cobalt, copper, lithium, rare earth elements, nickel, and phosphate.
To compile this list, the CESE drew on American and European methodologies. It provides an initial framework for considering critical and strategic resources for the Kingdom, but has no regulatory standing and cannot be considered definitive, explains the PCNS economist. He adds: “Regular updates to this list are necessary to account for global technological, economic, and geopolitical developments, as well as advances in mineral exploration and the identification of new deposits”.
Nevertheless, once this classification framework is developed, a comprehensive industrial strategy would be necessary to truly capitalize on these valuable resources. Otherwise, Morocco will continue to export its “gold mine” in its raw state, rather than using it as a lever of sovereignty.
Mineral? Ore? Rock? Metal?
Some refer to “critical ores” others to “critical minerals”. A mineral is a natural substance, generally solid and crystalline, that is a component of rocks, as is the case with rare earth elements or potash. An ore is a rock containing one or more useful minerals in sufficient quantities to be mined industrially. Finally, many metallic elements, such as cobalt, nickel, and copper, are also considered critical: these are metals obtained after refining and processing an ore.
Written in French by Salomé Krumenacher, edited in English by Amina Kadiri

- OPEC+'s 2027 oil quota review is delayed due to Middle East conflict, creating uncertainty in future production capacity
LONDON/MOSCOW: An OPEC+ review to help to determine members’ 2027 oil output quotas has been delayed after the US-Israeli war on Iran disrupted projects to expand capacity across the Middle East, throwing estimates of future production potential into uncertainty, said two sources close to the matter.
OPEC+, which comprises the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries plus Russia and other allies, had ordered its production capacity review for all members in late 2025 before setting 2027 quotas, with completion due by the end of September 2026.
The deadline has slipped, the sources said, with one saying the review is now expected to be completed by mid-November.
The OPEC producer group did not respond immediately to a request for comment.
Production capacity estimates in flux
The Middle East conflict has delayed projects that were due to boost production capacity in some OPEC+ countries, complicating estimates of how much oil they will be capable of pumping. Not all countries have submitted the data required for the review, the sources said without naming the countries.
The uncertainty complicates a politically sensitive exercise for OPEC+, with production capacity estimates likely to influence how much individual members are allowed to pump.
The review aims to provide an updated independent assessment of how much oil each member can produce sustainably, a key metric used in negotiations over output targets. Delays to planned capacity additions could affect assumptions underpinning those assessments and, potentially, members’ future quotas.
Countries whose assessed capacity is lower could face pressure for lower quotas while producers that have expanded capacity might seek higher allocations.
The United Arab Emirates, which had pushed for a higher quota from OPEC+ to reflect rising production capacity, left the alliance in May.
Iraq is also seeking a higher quota and has considered leaving OPEC, sources told Reuters in June.

articles.title: IWL Boss Challenges Gov’t on Liberia’s Critical Minerals Future - liberianobserver.com
articles.summary: IWL Boss Challenges Gov’t on Liberia’s Critical Minerals Future  liberianobserver.com
articles.full_text:
Integrity Watch Liberia Executive Director Harold Marvin Aidoo has challenged the government to put stronger safeguards in place before committing Liberia’s emerging critical-minerals sector to major investors, saying the country risks repeating its history of exporting valuable resources without building lasting wealth at home.
With global demand accelerating for lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, rare-earth elements and other minerals essential to batteries, electric vehicles and renewable-energy technologies, Aidoo says Liberia is entering an important investment cycle. But without stronger institutions and enforceable investment terms, he cautions, the country could repeat its iron-ore experience, exporting valuable resources while mining communities remain poor and the wider economy captures little of the wealth.
In a policy commentary released Thursday, titled “Liberia Must Not Miss the Critical Minerals Moment,” Aidoo called on government to publish the non-confidential findings of a China-supported mineral survey and establish the commercial potential of identified deposits before making major commitments to investors.
The survey has reportedly indicated the presence of lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese, rare-earth elements and other strategic minerals, although indications do not necessarily constitute commercially viable reserves.
“Liberia has another chance to turn mineral wealth into lasting prosperity,” Aidoo said, warning that without stronger extractive-sector governance, “valuable resources leave our shores while communities remain poor.”
Liberia’s iron-ore history, he said, offers a warning. Commercial production began at Bomi Hills in 1951, generating exports and government revenue but limited linkages with Liberian businesses, manufacturing and technical capacity.
“Railways and ports moved ore abroad, while the knowledge and industrial capacity needed to transform the wider economy remained insufficient,” he said.
Aidoo warned that the global transition to cleaner energy could reproduce the pattern if Liberia becomes primarily a supplier of raw minerals to industries elsewhere.
“Liberia might supply minerals for cleaner technologies overseas while absorbing environmental damage and receiving only a modest share of the value,” he said. “A green product does not guarantee a fair supply chain.”
He urged Liberia to engage multiple international partners while keeping national development priorities at the center of negotiations.
“The question for every partnership should be practical: what will Liberia gain beyond the export of ore?” he asked.
Future agreements, he said, should include measurable commitments on Liberian employment, skills development, local procurement, infrastructure, environmental protection and, where commercially viable, processing.
“Political friendship cannot substitute for a sound commercial bargain,” he said.
Aidoo also called for a national critical-minerals strategy linking mining to electricity, education, industry and trade. Liberia’s 2000 Minerals and Mining Law and 2010 Mineral Policy, he noted, predate the current global competition for energy-transition minerals.
The strategy should provide for transparent licensing, beneficial-ownership disclosure, public access to mining contracts and independent technical advice for lawmakers reviewing major agreements.
“Local procurement, training and processing commitments need deadlines, measurable targets and consequences for non-performance,” Aidoo said.
He also called for stronger revenue safeguards, including independent verification of mineral quality, production volumes and export values, as well as measures to detect under-invoicing and abusive related-party pricing.
“Without these safeguards, apparently attractive agreements can still leave the country collecting far less than it should,” he warned.
On value addition, Aidoo cautioned against assuming every deposit should result in a refinery.
“Liberia cannot demand a refinery for every deposit without considering electricity costs, water availability, environmental risks and markets,” he said.
Instead, he urged gradual development of commercially viable processing and greater local participation in geological, engineering, maintenance and logistics services.
Mining projects, he added, should contribute to electricity, roads, railways and ports that benefit communities and businesses beyond individual mines.
“Shared railways, ports and transmission infrastructure can create economic opportunities well beyond the mine,” he said.
Aidoo also stressed investment in universities, vocational institutions, apprenticeships and recognized qualifications to ensure Liberians gain technical and managerial expertise.
“Counting Liberians on payrolls is insufficient if technical knowledge and managerial authority remain elsewhere,” he said.
He further called for safeguards covering community consultation, water protection, grievance mechanisms and mine closure.
“The decisions taken before licences and long-term sales agreements are signed will shape what Liberia retains for decades,” Aidoo said. “We should use this period to verify our mineral potential, strengthen institutions and define the benefits investors must deliver.”
“Minerals are finite. Skills, productive infrastructure and capable institutions can outlast them,” he said. “Liberia’s goal should be to turn the resources beneath our soil into the capacity to build prosperity long after the mines close.”

articles.title: Beautiful Day – FIDs on LNG Canada Phase 2, Coastal GasLink Expansion to Boost Montney Production - RBN Energy
articles.summary: Beautiful Day – FIDs on LNG Canada Phase 2, Coastal GasLink Expansion to Boost Montney Production  RBN Energy
articles.full_text:
The big news this week may have been the final investment decision (FID) on LNG Canada’s Phase 2, but that announcement — spurred in part by recent changes in Canadian tax policy — will have even larger upstream impacts. For one thing, TC Energy will now move ahead with its plan to nearly double the capacity of the massive Coastal GasLink pipeline, which serves LNG Canada. Also, producers in northeastern British Columbia’s Montney Formation can now make firmer plans to significantly ramp up drilling-and-completion activity, an expansion that will have positive effects on condensate production for use in the Alberta oil sands. In today’s RBN blog, we’ll explain why the newly sanctioned LNG Canada expansion signals a “beautiful day” for a wide range of Western Canadian market players.

This course is designed to equip you with the knowledge and skills to effectively analyze the complexities of natural gas markets, flow analysis, and pipeline modeling. Join us online
October 21 | Online
As you all know by now, the consortium that co-owns the existing LNG Canada Phase 1 — Shell (the operator, with a 40% stake), Petronas (25%, with one-fifth of that implicitly held by MidOcean Energy), PetroChina Co. Ltd. (15%), Mitsubishi Corp. (15%) and Korea Gas Corp. (KOGAS, 5%) — has now reached FID on Phase 2. In the team’s September 28 announcement, they said that, like Phase 1 (orange diamond in Figure 1 below), the Phase 2 expansion at Kitimat, BC, will consist of two liquefaction trains and boast a capacity of 14 MMtpa, or about 1.8 Bcf/d. Phase 2 (checkered orange-and-white diamond), which is expected to come online in 2031-32, also will include an additional LNG storage tank, condensate tank and loading berth, as well as expanded utility and process systems.
Also as in Phase 1, the LNG produced by Phase 2 will be allocated to the five co-owners (Shell, Petronas, etc.) according to their ownership stakes in the project; the companies will be responsible for providing their share of feedgas from Montney production (more on that in a moment).
The LNG Canada team said the Phase 2 sanctioning will trigger implementation of an equity agreement with MNT Investments LP, a limited partnership of the economic development organizations of five First Nations neighboring LNG Canada’s operations: Gitga’at First Nation, Gitxaała Nation, Haisla Nation, Kitselas First Nation and Kitsumkalum. The agreement, first unveiled in July, calls for MNT Investments to invest up to C$1 billion (about US$705 million) to acquire a majority equity ownership interest in a special purpose entity that will purchase the LNG storage tank to be built as part of Phase 2. The asset will then be leased back to LNG Canada for the operational life of the project.
Chris Cooper, LNG Canada’s president and CEO, said in a statement that the Phase 2 expansion puts LNG Canada “on a trajectory to become one of the largest LNG facilities in the world” and helps move Canada “toward becoming one of the world’s top five LNG exporting nations.”
A final impetus for LNG Canada’s co-owners to sanction Phase 2 may well have been the Canadian government’s mid-September announcement of sweeping changes to federal tax policy that specifically encourage the development of capital-intensive energy projects, a topic we detailed in our weekly Canadian NATGAS Billboard. Most important, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Canada’s Department of Finance unveiled what they called a “Productivity Mega Deduction” that allows companies to write off 100% of eligible capital expenditures in Year 1 rather than depreciating them over decades via standard Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) rates.
Gasoline inventories are running unusually lean heading into fall. According to the EIA’s Weekly Petroleum Status Report (WPSR) for the week ended September 25, U.S. motor gasoline (mogas) stocks fell 1.7 MMbbl to just above 204 MMbbl, their lowest level since November 2014.
Eligible capex includes liquefaction equipment and gas pipelines, which brings us to the first, largest and most immediate knock-on effect of the LNG Canada Phase 2 announcement: the decision by TC Energy and its partners in the existing 2.5-Bcf/d Coastal GasLink (yellow line in Figure 1) to proceed with a project to double the capacity of the 416-mile pipeline from northeastern BC to Kitimat by adding five new compressor stations along its route. (TC Energy holds a 35% stake in Coastal GasLink and its financial partners, KKR and AIMCo, hold 32.5% each.)
The Coastal GasLink expansion will be constructed under a new execution model involving both LNG Canada and the Coastal GasLink team. Under an agreement reached in March 2025, LNG Canada will lead the project construction as the pipeline’s Phase 2 “execution manager” and the Coastal GasLink team will provide technical advisory services to LNG Canada and “remain the owner, operator and permit holder of the pipeline and associated facilities,” TC Energy said in a statement. “The commercial structure limits (Coastal GasLink’s) capital commitments and overall exposure to construction cost and schedule risks, consistent with TC Energy’s strategic priorities of disciplined execution, prudent capital allocation and maintaining financial strength.”
[Side note: The expanded Coastal GasLink system also will supply gas to Cedar LNG (striped-pink diamond in Figure 1), a planned 3.3-MMtpa (0.4 Bcf/d) floating LNG project now under construction, also in Kitimat. Other LNG projects under development include Ksi Lisims (checkered blue-and-white diamond) and Woodfibre LNG (striped-green diamond). See Shut Up and Drive for more.]
In addition to making the Coastal GasLink expansion a go, the LNG Canada Phase 2 FID also waved the green flag for gas-focused producers in the Montney. Now, with the certainty that another 1.8 Bcf/d of gas demand is being planned in Kitimat — and the pipeline from the Montney to Kitimat is being expanded — producers in the play can develop strategies for adding acreage and drilling (and completing) new wells, all with the aim of supplying the incremental gas that LNG Canada will need starting in five or six years.
Many of the Montney’s largest producers are affiliated with LNG Canada’s five co-owners. For example, Shell holds an 80% working interest in — and is the primary operator of — the Groundbirch joint venture (JV; upper pink-shaded area in Figure 2 below), with PetroChina, another LNG Canada owner, holding the other 20%. The JV controls nearly 300,000 mostly contiguous acres and produces more than 450 MMcf/d, most of which flows directly into Coastal GasLink to LNG Canada, as well as condensate (as Canada refers to natural gasoline) and other, lighter NGLs. [Shell’s legacy holdings in the region also include acreage in the Gold Creek area in northwestern Alberta (lower pink-shaded area), whose gas and liquids flow elsewhere.]
On September 2, Shell closed on its previously announced acquisition of ARC Resources. That deal gave Shell another 1.5 million acres in the Montney (aqua-shaded areas), a significant portion of which is near the Groundbirch acreage and Coastal GasLink’s origination point. Overall, ARC’s acreage produces about 1.5 Bcf/d of gas and 170 Mb/d of liquids. The ARC deal also gave Shell about 2 Bcf/d of gas processing capacity and 200 Mb/d of liquids-handling capacity in the Montney.
Petronas, which holds the second-largest stake in LNG Canada Phases 1 and 2 after Shell, is also a major player in Montney production; it operates — and owns a roughly 60% interest in — the North Montney Joint Venture (NMJV), which controls more than 800,000 acres in the play and currently produces more than 1 Bcf/d, much of it for LNG Canada. Also, Mitsubishi, with its 15% stake in LNG Canada, holds a 40% non-operating interest in the Cutbank Ridge Partnership (CRP), another large Montney producer operated by Ovintiv (which owns the other 60% of CRP).
The expected rise in Montney gas production to meet the feedgas needs of LNG Canada Phase 2 will have an important and lucrative side effect: a significant increase in associated condensate (i.e., natural gasoline) production in the liquids-rich play.
As we discussed in our Turn Me Loose series, Western Canadian crude oil production continues to hit all-time highs and is expected to continue growing into the 2030s. Almost all that growth is coming from the Alberta oil sands, and the bitumen that is not upgraded into synthetic crude oil must be diluted with vast amounts of diluent (condensate/natural gasoline) to flow through pipelines or be loaded into rail tank cars. Put simply, rising gas production in the Montney to serve an expanded LNG Canada — and other new LNG export facilities on the BC coast — will also sharply increase condensate production, a boon to oil sands producers that now rely heavily on piped-in natural gasoline from the U.S.
In sum, the recently announced FID on LNG Canada Phase 2 will have at least a few positive domino effects, including a major gas pipeline expansion, rising gas and liquids production in the Montney, and more, much-needed diluent for the oil sands.

articles.title: LNG Canada to use Chinese Steel on $33B expansion project in Kitmat, B.C. - Energy News Beat
articles.summary: LNG Canada to use Chinese Steel on $33B expansion project in Kitmat, B.C.  Energy News Beat
articles.full_text:
LNG Canada will again source major modules from a Chinese state-owned fabricator for its $33 billion Phase 2 expansion in Kitimat, B.C., even as Canadian primary steel producers idle lines and issue layoff notices under U.S. tariffs and persistent import pressure. Prime Minister Mark Carney has left the steel decision to the project owners while tightening quotas on foreign steel elsewhere and pursuing closer ties with the EU.
On September 28–29, 2026, the LNG Canada joint venture—Shell (40 percent), PETRONAS (25 percent), PetroChina (15 percent), Mitsubishi (15 percent), and KOGAS (5 percent)—took a final investment decision on Phase 2. The expansion adds two liquefaction trains, storage, and a loading berth, doubling nameplate capacity from 14 to 28 million tonnes per year. The federal government and project partners put the private investment at about $33 billion (roughly US$23 billion). Carney called it nation-building and said peak construction could support up to 4,000 jobs at the Kitimat site, with additional work on Coastal GasLink compressor stations. Permanent operating additions are far smaller: roughly 90 full-time roles and 150 contractor positions once complete, targeted for the early 2030s.
CBC News reported on October 2 that the joint venture will again buy large modules from China Offshore Oil Engineering Co. (COOEC), a unit of state-owned CNOOC. COOEC fabricated the Phase 1 process modules—35 modules totaling about 179,000 tons, delivered from its Qingdao yard. LNG Canada spokesperson Paul Hagel said the constraint is specialized fabrication capacity, not a preference for offshore steel: no Canadian yard can manufacture and deliver modules of this scale and complexity, and only five yards worldwide meet the requirements for space, quality systems, and marine access. Hagel added that new compressor stations on the pipeline are “targeting almost 15,000 tonnes of steel from Canadian suppliers or mills, representing approximately 70 per cent of the steel required for that work.”
Before the 2018 Phase 1 final investment decision, the project received a remission from anti-dumping and countervailing duties on fabricated industrial steel components from China. Officials at the time cited the absence of Canadian capacity and the risk that duties would affect the investment. Those duties later expired and were not renewed, so the same supplier path is open again. When asked at the announcement whether Phase 2 would use Canadian or Chinese steel, Carney said it was “a great question for the proponents” and that “there will be full opportunities to buy Canadian steel,” while adding that the choice was theirs.
Canadian mills under simultaneous pressure
The Kitimat decision lands while Canadian primary producers are losing their main export market. Canadian mills have historically sent more than half their output—and often over 90 percent of exports—to the United States. U.S. Section 232 tariffs on steel reached 50 percent in 2025. The Bank of Canada’s April 2026 Monetary Policy Report noted that steel exports have fallen by about half. A November 2025 Prime Minister’s Office backgrounder stated that employment in the steel sector had already dropped by roughly 1,000 jobs since the tariffs, against a base of about 23,000 direct steel jobs.
Concrete notices followed. In December 2025, Algoma Steel issued approximately 1,000 layoff notices tied to an accelerated shutdown of blast-furnace and coke operations in Sault Ste. Marie as it shifts to electric-arc production; the company had received substantial government financing partly to limit job losses. On September 28, 2026, Stelco (owned by Cleveland-Cliffs since a 2024 acquisition) said it would indefinitely idle cold-rolled and coated operations at Hamilton Works beginning around October 9, affecting up to 500 employees (union estimates put the Hamilton figure near 350). The company cited a nearly 25 percent drop in demand for those products in the second quarter of 2026 versus the 2024 quarterly average, plus continued import penetration. Carney called the Stelco move a betrayal of workers and pointed to employment-maintenance conditions attached to the Investment Canada Act approval of the Cleveland-Cliffs takeover. Energy News Beat covered the Stelco idling in detail on September 30.
Broader manufacturing payroll employment fell by 40,600 between December 2024 and December 2025, according to Statistics Canada, with durable-goods losses concentrated in Ontario. Earlier Energy News Beat reporting cited more than 51,000 manufacturing jobs shed in the twelve months after the first tariff wave, concentrated in Ontario’s auto and steel corridor, and economist Trevor Tombe’s estimate that the 50 percent tariffs put roughly 87,000 Canadian jobs at risk (about 52,000 direct).
Canada has responded with tighter tariff-rate quotas (non-free-trade-agreement partners cut to 20 percent of 2024 volumes, with a 50 percent surtax above quota), a 25 percent tariff on certain steel-derivative products, and melt-and-pour measures aimed at Chinese-origin content. Those steps have reduced some import volumes but have not restored the lost U.S. market.
Was the dumping and transshipment claim accurate?
Chinese steel overcapacity is long-standing and well documented. State-supported Chinese mills produce far more than domestic demand absorbs; the surplus is exported at prices that undercut producers in higher-cost jurisdictions, including Canada and the United States. OECD and industry data have repeatedly flagged global excess capacity measured in the hundreds of millions of tonnes, with China the largest source.
The narrower claim that Canada systematically served as a backdoor for Chinese steel into the United States is more contested. The Trump administration and U.S. industry witnesses have accused Canadian firms of transshipment or origin concealment. A May 2026 Justice Department settlement of $19 million with two Canadian companies resolved allegations (denied by the defendants) of failing to pay duties on steel from Asia and Europe, including China, and of alleged label removal. A White House report described a broader “Great Transshipment Scam” routing Chinese goods through third countries. Canadian Steel Producers Association representatives have rejected the premise that Canada is a dumping ground or transshipment hub, citing data that about 95 percent of steel shipped from Canada to the United States was melted and poured inside the USMCA region, and pointing to Canada’s own anti-dumping orders and surtaxes. Snopes reviewed the circulating social-media version of the claim and found company-level accusations and one settlement, but no court finding that the Canadian government itself ran a resale scheme.
Both things can be true at once: Chinese overcapacity and subsidized exports have pressured North American prices for years, isolated origin-fraud cases have occurred, and the integrated Canada–U.S. steel trade (largely North American melt-and-pour) has been disrupted by the 50 percent U.S. tariffs, producing measurable Canadian job losses and idled finishing capacity. The tariffs have also coincided with new U.S. mill investment announcements.
Carney’s alignment and the domestic gap
Carney’s government has advertised Buy Canadian preferences, quota tightening, and liquidity support for steel and lumber while simultaneously celebrating the LNG Canada expansion and pursuing deeper arrangements with the European Union, including discussion of an “associate” status built on CETA. On the flagship West Coast LNG project, the commercial decision remains with a consortium that includes a 15 percent PetroChina stake and that has already demonstrated it can obtain large modules from COOEC. The permanent operating jobs created in Kitimat are modest compared with the construction peak and the steel-sector losses already recorded in Ontario. Pipeline steel offers a partial offset; the core process modules do not.
LNG Canada’s capability argument is specific: Canada lacks yards that can build and load out modules of this size. That gap is real today. It is also the same gap cited for the Phase 1 duty remission. Whether policy treats that as a reason to keep importing finished modules from a Chinese state yard, or as a reason to build domestic heavy-fabrication capacity for the next round of energy projects, is the practical test of “Canada first” procurement on a $33 billion file.

articles.summary: Opencast And Open Pit Mining Excavators Market To 2035: Copper and Battery-Metal Demand Lifts Equipment Orders - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Abstract
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Opencast And Open Pit Mining Excavators market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global market for opencast and open pit mining excavators enters the 2026-2035 forecast period at a structural inflection point. Surface mining capital expenditure is being pulled higher by copper, lithium, nickel and iron ore output requirements tied to electrification, grid build-out and urbanisation, even as coal demand plateaus in several regions. At the same time, the installed fleet is ageing: many hydraulic excavators and electric rope shovels commissioned during the 2000s commodity supercycle are reaching replacement age, creating a visible renewal pipeline. The market is also bifurcating technologically.
Conventional diesel-powered hydraulic excavators remain the volume backbone, but battery-electric, trolley-assisted and hybrid machines are moving from trial to commercial deployment, supported by miners' Scope 1 emission targets. Autonomy, teleoperation and payload analytics are shifting from differentiators to procurement requirements. This report defines the market as heavy-duty excavating machinery for surface mining and quarrying, including hydraulic excavators, electric rope shovels, draglines, backhoe loaders, wheeled and crawler excavators, plus overburden and stockpile machinery, OEM equipment, aftermarket parts and distribution.
Underground mining machinery, general construction excavators, continuous surface miners, bucket-wheel excavators, drilling and boring machinery, conveyors and auxiliary haulage are excluded. The analysis covers 2012-2025 historical data and a 2026-2035 forecast, with value in USD, volume in tonnes and prices in USD per tonne.
The baseline scenario for 2026-2035 assumes global GDP growth in a moderate range, continued electrification investment, and no prolonged global recession. Under these conditions, opencast and open pit mining excavator demand is projected to grow at a compound annual growth rate of roughly 4.5% in value terms, with the market index reaching about 155 by 2035 from a 2025 base of 100. Volume growth will be slower than value growth because machine mix shifts toward larger, more expensive and more digitally equipped units, and because aftermarket parts and service capture a rising share of total spend.
The strongest demand pull comes from copper and other energy-transition minerals, where new mine development and brownfield expansion in Chile, Peru, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, the United States and Canada require high-capacity loading equipment. Iron ore replacement demand in Australia and Brazil provides a second pillar, while coal remains significant in India, Indonesia, China and parts of Africa but is expected to decline in Europe and North America. Quarrying and construction minerals extraction will grow in line with infrastructure and housing cycles, mainly in Asia-Pacific and Africa.
Supply-side constraints include long lead times for large castings, forged components and high-horsepower drivetrains, limited skilled labour for commissioning and maintenance, and tightening emissions rules in major mining jurisdictions. These factors will keep pricing firm and encourage OEMs to localise assembly and expand remanufacturing. The baseline does not assume a rapid, universal switch to zero-emission machines; instead, it assumes gradual adoption, with diesel and electric drive coexisting through 2035.
Demand Drivers and Constraints
Primary Demand Drivers
- Rising copper and energy-transition mineral output requirements, driven by electrification, renewable power and grid investment
- Ageing surface mining fleet and replacement cycles for hydraulic excavators and electric rope shovels commissioned during the 2000s supercycle
- Mine operators' productivity and cost-per-tonne pressure, supporting adoption of larger buckets, autonomy and payload analytics
- Decarbonisation commitments by major miners, accelerating trials and commercial deployment of battery-electric, trolley-assisted and hybrid excavators
- Infrastructure, housing and industrial construction demand in Asia-Pacific and Africa, supporting quarrying and construction minerals extraction
- Growth in aftermarket parts, remanufacturing and equipment rental as miners extend asset life and manage capital budgets
Potential Growth Constraints
- High capital cost of large mining excavators and uncertain commodity price cycles, which can delay or defer fleet orders
- Long lead times for specialised components such as large castings, forged parts and high-horsepower electric drive systems
- Shortage of skilled operators and maintenance technicians in remote mining regions, limiting effective utilisation of advanced machines
- Tightening emissions and safety regulations in key jurisdictions, raising compliance and retrofit costs for conventional diesel fleets
- Trade tensions, tariffs and local-content requirements that can disrupt cross-border supply chains and raise equipment prices
Demand Structure by End-Use Industry
End-Use Industry Demand Split (%)
Coal Mining (estimated share: 28%)
Coal mining remains the single largest end-use segment for opencast and open pit mining excavators, particularly in India, Indonesia, China, Australia and South Africa, where surface coal operations rely on large hydraulic excavators, electric rope shovels and draglines for overburden removal and coal loading. Through 2035, the segment's centre of gravity shifts further toward Asia, as European and North American coal consumption declines and mine closures reduce replacement demand in those regions. Demand-side indicators to watch include seaborne thermal and metallurgical coal prices, Indian domestic coal production targets, Indonesian export volumes and Chinese import policy.
In mature markets, miners are extending equipment life through rebuilds and aftermarket parts rather than buying new units, which supports the parts and service value chain. In growth markets, new mine development and expansion of existing pits require additional high-capacity loading equipment. The segment is also a testing ground for autonomy and electrification, as some coal miners seek to lower diesel exposure and improve safety in large pits. Overall, coal's share of the excavator market is expected to erode gradually, but it will remain a major demand pillar through 2035. Current trend: Stable to declining in Europe and North America, growing in India, Indonesia and parts of Africa.
Major trends: Shift of coal production growth toward India, Indonesia and parts of Africa, Mine closures and reduced replacement demand in Europe and North America, Growing use of rebuilds, remanufactured components and extended service contracts, Autonomy and teleoperation pilots in large surface coal pits, and Tighter emissions and dust-control rules affecting equipment specifications.
Representative participants: Coal India Limited, BHP Group, Glencore plc, Anglo American plc, Peabody Energy Corporation, and Adaro Energy Indonesia.
Metal Ore Mining (estimated share: 34%)
Metal ore mining is the most dynamic end-use segment for opencast and open pit mining excavators and is expected to account for the largest share of incremental demand through 2035. Copper is the anchor: electrification, renewable generation, grid expansion and electric vehicles all require large volumes of copper, and many new copper projects are open pit operations. Lithium, nickel and cobalt demand is also rising, though some lithium and nickel projects use different mining methods. Iron ore remains a major segment, especially in Australia and Brazil, where large hydraulic excavators and rope shovels load high-tonnage haul trucks.
Demand-side indicators include copper and iron ore prices, capital expenditure guidance from major miners, project permitting timelines and ore grade trends. As grades decline at mature mines, operators must move more material per unit of metal, which increases loading equipment requirements. This segment is also the primary adopter of autonomous haulage and loading, battery-electric and trolley-assisted machines, and digital fleet management systems. The result is a mix shift toward larger, more expensive and more technologically advanced excavators, supporting value growth above volume growth. Current trend: Strong growth, led by copper, lithium, nickel and iron ore.
Major trends: Copper and energy-transition mineral demand driving new mine development and expansion, Declining ore grades increasing material movement per unit of metal, Rapid adoption of autonomous haulage and loading systems, Battery-electric and trolley-assisted excavator trials at major mines, and Rising capital expenditure by diversified and copper-focused miners.
Representative participants: Freeport-McMoRan Inc, BHP Group, Rio Tinto Group, Vale S.A, Southern Copper Corporation, and Antofagasta plc.
Quarrying (estimated share: 18%)
Quarrying covers the extraction of crushed stone, sand, gravel and dimension stone for construction and industrial uses. It is a broad, fragmented segment with many small and mid-sized operators, and it relies heavily on hydraulic excavators, wheeled excavators and backhoe loaders rather than the largest mining shovels. Through 2035, quarrying demand for excavators will track infrastructure spending, housing construction and industrial investment, with Asia-Pacific and Africa showing the strongest growth and Europe and North America showing replacement-driven demand. Demand-side indicators include public infrastructure budgets, cement and aggregates consumption, and private construction activity.

articles.title: Shell approves USD 23 billion LNG Canada expansion in boost to Mark Carney’s energy push - internationalfinance.com
articles.summary: Shell approves USD 23 billion LNG Canada expansion in boost to Mark Carney’s energy push  internationalfinance.com
articles.full_text:
Shell and its partners have approved a USD 23 billion expansion of LNG Canada in British Columbia, doubling the facility’s production capacity and giving Prime Minister Mark Carney’s plan to turn the country into an energy superpower an endorsement.
The consortium reached a final investment decision on Phase 2 on Tuesday, committing CUSD 33 billion to add two liquefaction trains at the Kitimat terminal. The expansion will lift annual production from 14 million tonnes to 28 million tonnes, with commercial operations expected in the early 2030s.
Shell, which operates LNG Canada and holds a 40% stake, said the project would strengthen its integrated gas portfolio and connect Canadian resources with its global LNG trading and customer network. The company expects to receive nearly 6 million tonnes of additional LNG from Phase 2.
The remaining partners are Malaysia’s Petronas, with a 25% stake; PetroChina and Mitsubishi Corporation, each with 15%; and Korea Gas Corporation, with 5%. The project will primarily target Asian markets, where buyers are seeking diversified supplies amid heightened geopolitical and shipping risks.
For Ottawa, the decision is central to a broader effort to reduce Canada’s reliance on the US market and expand trade with Asia and Europe. Carney has set a target for Canada to export nearly 50 million tonnes of LNG annually by 2030 and has described the country as an energy superpower.
LNG Canada Phase 2 is one of the first major projects to be advanced through the government’s Major Projects Office, which was created to accelerate nationally significant infrastructure.
The project was referred to the office in September 2025, and the government has said the process is intended to provide investors with greater certainty while maintaining regulatory standards.
Carney’s government estimates Phase 2 will generate more than 4,000 construction jobs. LNG Canada said nearly USD 5 billion in contracts and procurement had already gone to Indigenous-owned and local businesses across the region.
The Haisla Nation’s traditional territory hosts the project, which includes an Indigenous equity agreement with five First Nations.
The expansion also strengthens the case for upstream investment in western Canada.
The 670-kilometre Coastal GasLink pipeline transports natural gas from the Montney formation in British Columbia and Alberta to Kitimat, British Columbia.
TC Energy is now moving ahead with an expansion of the pipeline, including five new compressor stations, to support the additional LNG capacity.
Shell’s commitment follows its acquisition of ARC Resources, a major Canadian oil and gas producer with extensive Montney assets. The deal, announced in April and completed this year, increased Shell’s exposure to Canadian gas and gives the company resources that can support its LNG business.
LNG Canada’s economics closely align with its Pacific location. Canadian construction costs are higher than those of some US Gulf Coast projects, but the Kitimat terminal is closer to major Asian customers.
Shell has argued that cheap Montney gas and shorter shipping distances help offset higher construction costs.
The timing is also significant.
Shell expects global LNG demand to rise from 422 million tonnes a year in 2025 to nearly 700 million tonnes by 2050, an increase of about 65%.
Asian markets are expected to account for a substantial share of demand as economies expand and seek reliable supplies.
The project could also alter the economics for Canadian gas producers. Western Canada has faced periods of weak natural gas prices partly because production has grown faster than pipeline capacity.
A second LNG outlet on the Pacific coast could provide producers with greater access to international markets and potentially narrow the discount between Canadian gas and global prices, although the effect will depend on supply, demand and infrastructure constraints.
The expansion is controversial.
Environmental groups have raised concerns about the project’s greenhouse gas emissions and the longer-term role of fossil fuel infrastructure. Critics have also questioned whether rising LNG exports are compatible with Canada’s climate objectives.
Ottawa argues that Phase 2 will be among the lower-emissions LNG projects globally, while Shell says LNG can play a role in meeting energy demand and replacing higher-emissions fuels in some markets.
The company says Phase 2 is expected to generate returns above the hurdle rate for its integrated gas business.
For Canada, however, the investment represents more than an expansion of one terminal. It is a test of whether the country can translate its natural-resource base into a larger export platform while attracting private capital, Indigenous participation and infrastructure investment.
With Phase 2 now sanctioned, LNG Canada is set to become one of the world’s largest LNG facilities. The project, according to Carney, is concrete proof that Canada can expand its export capacity beyond its usual trade route with the US.
It provides Shell and its partners with a strategic Pacific gateway for Canadian gas and a long-term position in a growing LNG market.
