articles.full_text:
ConocoPhillips has agreed to buy one million metric tons per annum (MMtpa) of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Venture Global Inc for 20 years from 2030.
"This agreement reflects continued market confidence in our proven ability to deliver reliable, low-cost U.S. LNG quickly and at scale", Venture Global chief executive Mike Sabel said in a brief statement.
For its LNG supply business, ConocoPhillips aims to offtake 10-15 MMtpa, according to a company statement September 8, 2025 announcing a 20-year agreement for one MMtpa from NextDecade Corp's Rio Grande LNG project in Texas.
Earlier last year Houston-based ConocoPhillips agreed to buy four MMtpa over 20 years from phase 2 of Sempra's Port Arthur LNG project in Texas. ConocoPhillips had already signed up for five MMtpa over 20 years from phase 1, in which it also owns a 30 percent stake.
ConocoPhillips says on its website it has about 10 MMtpa of offtakes in North America, with initial deliveries between 2026 and 2031.
"From a regasification and sales perspective, we have placed the five MTPA [million metric tons per annum] of Port Arthur LNG Phase 1 offtake through regasification capacity agreements in Europe and direct sales agreements to Asia", ConocoPhillips says. "We continue to progress discussions across all major LNG producing and consuming regions and markets to further add high-quality positions to our portfolio".
Arlington, Virginia-based LNG developer Venture Global, meanwhile, says on its website it has over 100 MMtpa of LNG capacity already in production, under construction or under plan.
Just a few days ago Venture Global said it had executed a new agreement to supply 0.5 MMtpa of United States LNG to China Gas Holdings Ltd for 20 years from 2030.
"This SPA [sale and purchase agreement] brings Venture Global's current long-term offtake with China Gas to 2.5 Mtpa under 20-year SPAs supplied across Venture Global's portfolio", Venture Global said September 14.
Three years ago the companies signed two SPAs, each with a term of 20 years.
"Under the deals, China Gas will buy one million tonnes per annum of LNG on a free on board basis from Plaquemines LNG and another one MTPA from the CP2 LNG export facility, both in Louisiana", said a joint statement February 23, 2023.
The project in Plaquemines Parish is preparing to start "commercial operation" by the fourth quarter, though Venture Global had already announced the start of shipments December 26, 2024.
"We are in the final stages of construction, commissioning and assurance testing required in advance of COD [commercial operations date] of our Plaquemines Project Phase 1, and the team is working tirelessly to safely complete the remaining phase 1 scopes", Venture Global said in its quarterly statement August 10. "As recently communicated with our phase 1 customers, we are pleased to reaffirm that we are targeting Plaquemines Project Phase 1 COD in Q4 2026 and Plaquemines Project Phase 2 COD in mid-2027".
Venture Global added, "We continue to progress early development of the Plaquemines Expansion Phase 1, following our permit applications filed with FERC [Federal Energy Regulatory Commission] and the DOE [Department of Energy] late last year. Subject to regulatory approvals, we are targeting FID [final investment decision] in the first half of 2027 and first LNG in 2029".
On March 13 DOE approved an immediate 13 percent increase in exports from Plaquemines LNG. "With today's order, Plaquemines LNG is now authorized to immediately export a total of 3.85 Bcfd [billion cubic feet per day] to both FTA [free trade agreement] and non-FTA countries", the department said.
CP2, meanwhile, is under construction. CP2 holds FTA and non-FTA authorization to ship about 28 MMtpa or 1.45 trillion cubic feet a year of gas equivalent. Venture Global expects to put the project into production next year.
"During the quarter, we filed for CP2 brownfield expansion permits with FERC and non-FTA export authorization at DOE", Venture Global said in its quarterly statement. "Subject to regulatory approval, we are targeting FID on the CP2 Expansion in early 2027 with first production in late 2028".

Fluor will recognize its US$7.5 billion portion of the multibillion-dollar contract during the third quarter of fiscal 2026. The joint venture will provide engineering, procurement, fabrication, construction and commissioning services for the expansion.

LNG Canada began producing LNG in June 2025, with facility handover completed in October 2025.
Most ERP systems are built for accounting, inventory, and operations. Construction demands much more.
Phase 2 construction is being executed by JGC Fluor BC LNG II JV, a Canadian joint venture owned equally by Fluor Canada Ltd. and JGC Constructors (No2) BC Ltd.
The LNG Canada ownership group consists of Shell with a 40% interest, PETRONAS with 25%, PetroChina with 15%, Mitsubishi Corporation with 15% and KOGAS with 5%.
The project site is located on Canada's west coast and has access to natural gas resources and a deepwater harbor that remains ice-free. Those characteristics support the facility's role in LNG export operations and provide marine access for shipping.
The Phase 2 award adds a major LNG construction program to Fluor's energy portfolio and extends the joint venture's involvement at the Kitimat facility following completion of Phase 1. articles.title: European drought and heat hits grain farmers harder than feared – costs up to €3.2 billion - Energy & Climate Intelligence Unit | ECIU
articles.summary: European drought and heat hits grain farmers harder than feared – costs up to €3.2 billion  Energy & Climate Intelligence Unit | ECIU
articles.full_text:
New analysis using industry forecasts suggests the grain harvest will be down over 16 million tonnes after the hottest summer on record in Western Europe.
Last updated:
The summer drought and heatwaves drove a 16.7 million tonne reduction in forecast grain production between June and September this year – 8 million tonnes more than previously forecast in July
- At current prices, this net loss of grain would be worth €3.2 billion
- France was the worst hit country losing 5.8m tonnes (€1.47bn), followed by Hungary (3.1m tonnes/€723m), the UK (3m tonnes/€527m), Germany (2.5m tonnes/€398m) and Spain (1.2m tonnes/€220m)
New analysis [1] from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) estimates that the record-breaking European heat and drought is likely to cost European farmers around €3.2 billion. The analysis is based on the latest September forecast from COCERAL [2], the industry body representing the cereals, oilseeds, rice and olive oil sectors, and compares this to their June forecast.
Compared to that June forecast [3], European production of grains such as wheat, maize and barley is estimated to be down by 16.7 million tonnes after extreme heat affected kernel filling for wheat and maize pollination and reduced the maize area. This increases the losses from COCERAL’s ‘extraordinary’ July forecast [4] by a further 8 million tonnes. Previous ECIU analysis [5] estimated that this would have cost €1.8 billion. The increase to €3.2 billion illustrates the relentless heat and drought that continued to hit western, southern and central Europe throughout July and August. 
Tom Lancaster, farming analyst at ECIU said, “This summer’s extreme heat and drought has been unprecedented, costing Europe production equivalent to the entire grain output of Italy, Belgium and the Netherlands combined. At a time of geopolitical uncertainty, climate change is reducing our continents productive capacity and food security when we can least afford it.
“With Europe warming at twice the global average [6], climate losses like this are just a sign of things to come if we don’t move faster to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to net zero to bring our climate back into balance. To safeguard our food security in the short term however, governments and business will have to invest in soil health and other regenerative farming measures to boost the resilience of Europe’s farms in the face of these climate impacts.”  
This summer marked the hottest summer on record for western Europe as well as large swathes of southern and central Europe [7]. In the UK, July was the driest on record in England and Wales, adding to extreme heat in May and June that reduced the harvest by 3 million tonnes, costing farmers there €527m or £452m. 
France was the worst affected country, with a net loss of 5.8 million tonnes, valued at €1.47 billion, with Hungary, Germany and Spain also losing significant volumes of production. Excluding upward revisions in forecast production in Romania, Bulgaria, Poland and Sweden, losses increase from €3.2 billion to €4.1 billion, which more accurately reflects the losses experienced by farmers across Western and Central Europe. 
French cereal farmer Sébastien Neveux, who farms 300 hectares in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region said, “This year, on my farm, all my crops have been affected. Winter crops have been the least affected, despite yield losses of 25 per cent. But for spring and summer crops, it’s quite simply a disaster. Sunflowers, for example, yielded 0.7 tonnes per hectare instead of the usual 1.5 to 2, which is a 60 per cent loss.
“With heatwaves starting as early as May, I can no longer find a solution. Especially as these climate impacts are compounding the geopolitical crises that are driving our costs through the roof. And on top of these recurring crises, market prices are far too low to cover our production costs.”
European diesel and fertiliser prices [8] spiked after the Iran war and remain elevated, as the volatile price of fossil fuels significantly increased farmers’ costs. Scientists at World Weather Attribution (WWA) have found that the June heatwave would have been ‘virtually impossible’ fifty years ago without climate change [9]. 
The impact of this summer has been felt well beyond the grain harvest, with the European Commission Joint Research Centre [10] recently estimating that yields for soybeans are down 15%, potatoes 7% and sugar beet 11%, with reductions in grass growth also hitting livestock farms. They concluded that the impact on total production is expected to be even greater than these yield losses would suggest, with some of the hardest-hit crops so severely damaged that harvesting is no longer economically viable and fields have been abandoned.

articles.title: UK Sanctions Five LNG Carriers Linked to Russia’s Arctic Fleet - Ships & Ports
articles.summary: UK Sanctions Five LNG Carriers Linked to Russia’s Arctic Fleet  Ships & Ports
articles.full_text:
The United Kingdom has sanctioned five liquefied natural gas (LNG) carriers as part of a new package targeting Russia’s maritime “shadow fleet” and efforts to expand its Arctic LNG export capacity.
The vessels named in the October 1 sanctions notice are Chaivo, Portovyy, Aleksey Kosygin, Konstantin Posyet and Pyotr Stolypin.
The measures prohibit their operation and chartering, bar them from UK ports and restrict maritime services linked to the ships.
Three of the vessels — Aleksey Kosygin, Konstantin Posyet and Pyotr Stolypin — are Russian-built Arc7 ice-class LNG carriers intended for the Arctic LNG 2 project.
Pyotr Stolypin is still being prepared for sea trials at the Zvezda shipyard, making its designation notable as the UK moves to constrain future Russian LNG shipping capacity.
Arc7 vessels are designed to navigate heavy Arctic ice without an escort, supporting LNG shipments along the Northern Sea Route.
Konstantin Posyet, delivered this year, has already sailed the route to Arctic LNG 2 and loaded a cargo at the Utrenniey terminal.
The other two carriers, Chaivo and Portovyy, are older LNG tankers. The UK said Chaivo has carried Russian LNG to third countries, while Portovyy, operated by Gazprom, made an unusual voyage this summer from the Baltic through the Northern Sea Route to China.
The wider sanctions package covers 23 individuals and entities and eight vessels, including oil tankers and bunkering vessels.
The measures come as Britain tightens restrictions on Russian LNG. Existing licences for transporting Russian LNG have been extended temporarily to support energy security in Japan and South Korea, while the UK’s ban on maritime and insurance services connected with Russian LNG exports is due to take effect on 1 January 2027.

CARSON CITY, Nev. October 01, 2026 - American Lithium Minerals, Inc. (OTC: AMLM) has completed its PCAOB-standard financial audit, clearing an important financial-reporting hurdle as the multi-commodity exploration company moves toward its planned OTCQB Venture Market uplisting in the fourth quarter of 2026.
The completed audit satisfies one of the core eligibility requirements associated with OTCQB, while the actual uplisting remains subject to additional requirements and completion of the application process. For AMLM, the move could represent an important capital-markets transition, potentially expanding brokerage access, increasing market visibility and improving the company's ability to pursue future financing and strategic initiatives.
Today, American Lithium Minerals, Inc. (OTC: AMLM) is featured alongside Advasa Holdings, Inc. (NASDAQ: ADBT), American Fusion Inc. (OTCQB: AMFN), Genius Group Limited (NYSE American: GNS), and SunHydrogen, Inc. (OTCQB: HYSR), as investors monitor actively traded emerging-growth companies across critical minerals, advanced energy, technology and clean-energy markets.
AMLM Is Becoming Much More Than a Lithium Story
Although American Lithium Minerals is frequently grouped with lithium exploration , the company's current portfolio is considerably broader.
AMLM now describes itself as a multi-commodity critical minerals and precious metals exploration company, with 11 active project interests providing exposure to gold, silver, copper, lithium and rare earth elements (REEs) across multiple international mining jurisdictions.
Its portfolio includes the Higginsville Gold Project in Western Australia, silver and copper exploration interests in Chile, rare earth and polymetallic interests in Quebec, and lithium properties in Nevada, among other projects.
That diversification places AMLM at the intersection of several major resource themes: gold and precious metals, copper electrification demand, lithium and battery metals, rare earth elements, critical minerals, artificial intelligence infrastructure, defense supply chains and energy security.
Rather than depending entirely on one commodity cycle, AMLM's strategy provides potential exposure to multiple metals and geographic regions. That does not eliminate exploration or financing risk, but it broadens the number of potential catalysts available to the company.
Near $0.07 Creates a Valuation Story to Watch
AMLM shares have recently traded around $0.07, while the 's 52-week trading range has extended to approximately $0.265 at the high end.
That means the shares currently trade roughly 74% below their 52-week high, creating a sizable valuation gap for investors evaluating whether the company's expanded asset portfolio and improving corporate structure are being fully reflected in its market capitalization.
The company also previously reported $18.68 million in total assets and $17.74 million in stockholders' equity as of June 30, 2026, following mineral-property acquisitions and strategic investments.
Those figures add another dimension to the valuation discussion. While they do not establish that AMLM shares are intrinsically worth a particular price—and exploration assets carry significant valuation uncertainty—the combination of a roughly $0.07 share price, expanded asset base, 11 project interests and completed PCAOB audit creates a potentially significant valuation disconnect for speculative resource investors to monitor.
OTCQB Could Become the Next Major Corporate Catalyst
The planned OTCQB uplisting could become particularly important because the OTCQB Venture Market generally provides greater transparency and market visibility than the basic OTC tier.
For AMLM, management expects the move to potentially provide broader investor access, improved market liquidity, real-time market data availability and increased institutional visibility, while establishing a stronger platform for future corporate financing initiatives.
The company currently trades on OTC Markets' Basic Market. Consequently, completion of the planned Q4 uplisting would represent an actual change in AMLM's market tier rather than simply an administrative update.
Multiple Catalysts Could Shape AMLM's Next Phase
The investment story heading into the remainder of 2026 therefore extends well beyond lithium.
Investors now have several developments to monitor: completion of the OTCQB uplisting process, advancement of the company's 11 mineral project interests, additional exploration results, project-level transactions, potential partnerships and financing initiatives.
AMLM remains an exploration-stage company, meaning significant risks remain. Mineral resources require substantial capital to explore and potentially develop, commodity prices can fluctuate sharply, and neither exploration success nor completion of the OTCQB uplisting is guaranteed.
Nevertheless, the company's evolution is becoming increasingly measurable.
AMLM has moved from being viewed primarily as a small lithium explorer toward building a geographically diversified gold, silver, copper, lithium, rare earth and critical minerals portfolio. Now, with its PCAOB audit completed and a Q4 2026 OTCQB uplisting targeted, the capital-markets side of that transformation is beginning to advance as well.
At approximately $0.07 per share versus a 2026 high near $0.265, the question for investors is whether the market will eventually assign greater value to AMLM's expanding mineral portfolio and improving reporting infrastructure. If management successfully executes its planned uplisting and advances its underlying projects, a renewed test of higher valuation levels would become an important development for the stock to watch.

articles.title: Alaska LNG could cost more than double Gulf Coast rivals, raising questions over economics - WDEZ
articles.summary: Alaska LNG could cost more than double Gulf Coast rivals, raising questions over economics  WDEZ
articles.full_text:
By Curtis Williams
HOUSTON, Oct 1 (Reuters) – US President Donald Trump’s push to steer $54 billion of South Korean investment into Alaska LNG is putting a fresh focus on a 20 million-ton-a-year export project that would cost more than twice as much as a comparable US Gulf Coast plant.
Trump unveiled the plan on Wednesday as part of a broader $200 billion South Korean package. Seoul quickly said it had not yet decided whether to fund Alaska LNG and would first review the project’s commercial viability.
“The question is whether Asian buyers are willing to pay a premium in exchange for security of supply. So far, we have not seen evidence of that,” said Jason Feer, head of business intelligence at Poten & Partners.
Lead developer Glenfarne Group estimates Alaska LNG will cost $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion. That works out to roughly $2.2 billion to $2.7 billion per million metric tons per annum of capacity, by far the highest of any US export project ever proposed.
By comparison, the wave of US LNG projects approved since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has generally been built at an average cost of about $1 billion per mtpa or less.
Cheniere Energy’s Corpus Christi Stage 3 expansion was estimated to cost about $8 billion for 10.5 mtpa of additional capacity, or roughly $760 million per mtpa.
Venture Global’s Plaquemines LNG project represented approximately $21 billion of investment for 20 mtpa, while NextDecade’s Rio Grande LNG and Woodside Energy’s Louisiana LNG are also near the $1 billion-per-mtpa threshold.
Gulf Coast export terminals tap extensive networks supplying shale gas from Texas, Louisiana and Appalachia. Alaska LNG would instead require an 800-mile (1,287-km) pipeline from the North Slope — a region in northern Alaska between the Brooks Range mountains and the Arctic Ocean — to Nikiski, estimated to cost $13.2 billion to $16.9 billion.
In addition to the pipeline, the project requires a large treatment plant on the North Slope before gas can be moved south for export. Glenfarne’s latest estimates place the cost of the treatment facility at $7.7 billion to $9.2 billion and the liquefaction terminal itself at $23.6 billion to $28.4 billion.
Alex Munton, director of global gas and LNG research at Rapidan Energy Group, said the project “may not be able to meet commercial thresholds for investment.”
Glenfarne did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On Wednesday, CEO Brendan Duval said Trump’s announcement would help bring “together the capital needed to accelerate Alaska LNG to a final investment decision and construction.”
Supporters say Alaska LNG’s location offers a strategic advantage because cargoes would reach key Asian importers such as Japan, South Korea and Taiwan significantly faster than Gulf Coast shipments, lowering shipping costs.
“Asia needs stable, secure supplies of gas and for that they may be willing to pay a premium,” said Jack Weixel at East Daley Analytics. He noted, however, that Canadian projects in the region could have advantages over Alaska LNG.
“These LNG developers should be looking at any and all options as the global market for natural gas, particularly among non-OECD nations, grows,” he said. “But, some will work better than others.”
(Reporting by Curtis Williams in Houston; Editing by Nathan Crooks and Bill Berkrot)
